key_insight: Stern-sculling propulsion is driven by two distinct hydrodynamic mechanisms: lift during lateral strokes and added-mass effects during backward strokes, with peak propulsive efficiency around 65% at intermediate speed.
engineering_relevance: The results help quantify when this traditional human-powered propulsion method is most effective, offering design and operating guidance for low-speed marine propulsion systems.
method: Continuously measured oar kinematics over a broad range of boat speeds
Recorded boat motion and forces acting on the oar
Separated propulsive contributions from lateral and backward stroke phases
evidence_signal: The study combines continuous experimental measurements across multiple boat speeds to compute propulsive efficiency as a function of speed, revealing a peak near 65% and a drop to about 25% at higher speeds.
watch_item: The reported efficiency is speed-dependent and falls substantially at higher speeds, so conclusions should not be generalized beyond the tested operating range.
paper_title: Hydrodynamics and propulsive efficiency of stern-sculling propulsion
